claim: The efficient knock-in of large DNA fragments to label endogenous proteins remains especially challenging in non-dividing cells such as neurons.
source: The efficient knock-in of large DNA fragments to label endogenous proteins remains especially challenging in non-dividing cells such as neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known challenge in the field.

claim: TKIT is a novel CRISPR/Cas9 based approach for efficient and precise genomic knock-in.
source: We developed Targeted Knock-In with Two (TKIT) guides as a novel CRISPR/Cas9 based approach for efficient, and precise, genomic knock-in.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper describing the new method developed.

claim: TKIT is resistant to INDEL mutations through targeting non-coding regions.
source: Through targeting non-coding regions TKIT is resistant to INDEL mutations.
evidence: This is a key feature of the method described in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the paper.

claim: TKIT can label endogenous synaptic proteins with various tags with efficiencies up to 42% in mouse primary cultured neurons.
source: We demonstrate TKIT labeling of endogenous synaptic proteins with various tags, with efficiencies up to 42% in mouse primary cultured neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H showing 41.7% efficiency for GFP-gephyrin.

claim: TKIT can label AMPAR subunits with Super Ecliptic pHluorin in vivo using in utero electroporation or viral injections in mice.
source: Utilizing in utero electroporation or viral injections in mice TKIT can label AMPAR subunits with Super Ecliptic pHluorin, enabling visualization of endogenous AMPARs in vivo using two-photon microscopy.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 5 and 6 showing in vivo imaging results.

claim: TKIT enables visualization of endogenous AMPARs in vivo using two-photon microscopy.
source: Utilizing in utero electroporation or viral injections in mice TKIT can label AMPAR subunits with Super Ecliptic pHluorin, enabling visualization of endogenous AMPARs in vivo using two-photon microscopy.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 5C, 5D, and 6F showing two-photon imaging of SEP-tagged AMPARs.

claim: TKIT can be used to assess the mobility of endogenous AMPARs using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching.
source: We further use TKIT to assess the mobility of endogenous AMPARs using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7E-F showing FRAP experiments with SEP-GluA1.

claim: TKIT can be used to tag AMPARs in rat neurons, demonstrating precise genome editing in another model organism.
source: Finally, we show that TKIT can be used to tag AMPARs in rat neurons, demonstrating precise genome editing in another model organism and highlighting the broad potential of TKIT as a method to visualize endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7A-D showing TKIT-mediated KI in rat neurons.

claim: Endogenous protein labeling removes the dependence on specific antibodies which require extensive validation.
source: First, it removes the dependence on specific antibodies which require extensive validation.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of endogenous protein labeling in the introduction.

claim: Introducing fluorescent tags circumvents difficulties of antibodies physically accessing their targets, such as core components of the postsynaptic density (PSD).
source: Second, introducing fluorescent tags circumvents difficulties of antibodies physically accessing their targets, such as core components of the postsynaptic density (PSD), in which the antibody epitopes can be sterically occluded by other proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of genetic tagging in the introduction.

claim: Genetic tagging with fluorescent proteins is compatible with longitudinal imaging in live tissue in vitro and in vivo.
source: Third, genetic tagging with fluorescent proteins is compatible with longitudinal imaging in live tissue in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage in the introduction and demonstrated in the in vivo imaging experiments.

claim: Tagging endogenous proteins prevents potential confounds of protein mis-localization following overexpression and preserves the natural transcriptional and posttranscriptional regulation of the gene.
source: Finally, tagging endogenous proteins prevents potential confounds of protein mis-localization following overexpression and preserves the natural transcriptional and posttranscriptional regulation of the gene.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of endogenous tagging in the introduction.

claim: The discovery of CRISPR/Cas9 changed the gene editing field.
source: The discovery of CRISPR/Cas9 changed the gene editing field (Cho et al., 2013; Cong et al., 2013; Doudna and Charpentier, 2014; Hsu et al., 2014; Jinek et al., 2012; Mali et al., 2013; Sander and Joung, 2014), making genome editing much easier, faster, and cheaper.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational CRISPR papers.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 technology made genome editing much easier, faster, and cheaper.
source: The discovery of CRISPR/Cas9 changed the gene editing field (Cho et al., 2013; Cong et al., 2013; Doudna and Charpentier, 2014; Hsu et al., 2014; Jinek et al., 2012; Mali et al., 2013; Sander and Joung, 2014), making genome editing much easier, faster, and cheaper.
evidence: This is a widely accepted fact in the field supported by citations.

claim: Generating transgenic knock-in organisms is still relatively time-consuming and considered low throughput, especially in rodents.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 technology has facilitated this approach; however, it is still relatively time-consuming and considered low throughput, especially in rodents.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current approaches in the introduction.

claim: Having knock-in in all cells in an organism can be problematic in dense tissues.
source: In addition, having knock-in (KI) in all cells in an organism can be problematic in dense tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of whole-organism knock-in approaches.

claim: Methods to enable genome editing in single or a relatively sparse population of cells are highly desirable.
source: Therefore, methods to enable genome editing in single or a relatively sparse population of cells are highly desirable.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for developing TKIT.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing strategies traditionally rely on homology-dependent recombination (HDR).
source: Such CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing strategies traditionally rely on homology-dependent recombination (HDR) (Lombardo et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013); however, HDR does not work efficiently in post-mitotic cells, such as neurons (Mao et al., 2008; Nishiyama et al., 2017; Orthwein et al., 2015; Saleh-Gohari and Helleday, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing HDR-based methods.

claim: HDR does not work efficiently in post-mitotic cells, such as neurons.
source: Such CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing strategies traditionally rely on homology-dependent recombination (HDR) (Lombardo et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013); however, HDR does not work efficiently in post-mitotic cells, such as neurons (Mao et al., 2008; Nishiyama et al., 2017; Orthwein et al., 2015; Saleh-Gohari and Helleday, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to papers demonstrating the inefficiency of HDR in neurons.

claim: In post-mitotic cells researchers have adopted methods based on non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
source: Consequently, in post-mitotic cells researchers have adopted methods based on non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) (Bétermier et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2019; Lieber, 2010; Suzuki et al., 2016; Willems et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing NHEJ-based methods.

claim: NHEJ-based approaches have achieved higher KI efficiency in neurons compared to HDR-based methods.
source: Such approaches have achieved higher KI efficiency in neurons compared to HDR-based methods.
evidence: This is stated as a known advantage of NHEJ-based methods.

claim: NHEJ-based approaches directly edit the coding sequence of the target gene, possibly causing INDEL mutations.
source: However, these approaches directly edit the coding sequence of the target gene, possibly causing (insertion or deletion) INDEL mutations, which commonly occur at CRISPR/Cas9 mediated editing sites (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing NHEJ-based methods and supported by citation.

claim: INDEL mutations commonly occur at CRISPR/Cas9 mediated editing sites.
source: However, these approaches directly edit the coding sequence of the target gene, possibly causing (insertion or deletion) INDEL mutations, which commonly occur at CRISPR/Cas9 mediated editing sites (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suzuki et al., 2016.

claim: INDEL mutations are especially a concern if the tag is not introduced at the C-terminal portion of the protein.
source: This is especially a concern if the tag is not introduced at the C-terminal portion of the protein.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: Even when KI proceeds as planned with existing methods, the deletion or addition of some amino acids flanking the tag is unavoidable.
source: Furthermore, even when the KI proceeds as planned, the deletion or addition of some amino acids flanking the tag is unavoidable, and the exact site of KI is still dependent on a (protospacer-adjacent motif) PAM and reliable guide to be present at the right place.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing NHEJ-based methods.

claim: The exact site of KI with existing methods is dependent on a PAM and reliable guide to be present at the right place.
source: Furthermore, even when the KI proceeds as planned, the deletion or addition of some amino acids flanking the tag is unavoidable, and the exact site of KI is still dependent on a (protospacer-adjacent motif) PAM and reliable guide to be present at the right place.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: TKIT utilizes two guide RNAs located in non-coding regions upstream and downstream of the coding sequence to be edited.
source: To address these problems, we designed a new strategy – Targeted Knock-In with Two (TKIT) guides – to enable precise genome editing by utilizing two guide RNAs located in non-coding regions upstream and downstream of the coding sequence to be edited.
evidence: This is the core design principle of TKIT described in the introduction.

claim: TKIT protects from INDEL mutations within the coding region.
source: This strategy protects from INDEL mutations within the coding region and enables absolute control over the sequence surrounding the KI site.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of TKIT.

claim: TKIT enables absolute control over the sequence surrounding the KI site.
source: This strategy protects from INDEL mutations within the coding region and enables absolute control over the sequence surrounding the KI site.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of TKIT.

claim: Since the coding region is not being targeted directly with TKIT, there are fewer limitations during the selection of potential guide RNAs.
source: In addition, since the coding region is not being targeted directly, we have fewer limitations during the selection of potential guide RNAs, increasing the availability of high-score guides and lowering the likelihood of off-target editing.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TKIT's design.

claim: TKIT increases the availability of high-score guides and lowers the likelihood of off-target editing.
source: In addition, since the coding region is not being targeted directly, we have fewer limitations during the selection of potential guide RNAs, increasing the availability of high-score guides and lowering the likelihood of off-target editing.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TKIT's design.

claim: Super Ecliptic pHluorin (SEP) is a pH dependent GFP variant.
source: In this study, we have used TKIT to KI Super Ecliptic pHluorin (SEP), a pH dependent GFP variant (Lin and Huganir, 2007; Miesenböck et al., 1998), and other protein tags to the N-terminus of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl D-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptor subunits, which form glutamate receptors responsible for the majority of excitatory transmission in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing SEP.

claim: AMPA and NMDA receptor subunits form glutamate receptors responsible for the majority of excitatory transmission in the brain.
source: In this study, we have used TKIT to KI Super Ecliptic pHluorin (SEP), a pH dependent GFP variant (Lin and Huganir, 2007; Miesenböck et al., 1998), and other protein tags to the N-terminus of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl D-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptor subunits, which form glutamate receptors responsible for the majority of excitatory transmission in the brain.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: TKIT provides an efficient, easy to use, and readily scalable approach for the tagging of endogenous proteins.
source: Thus, TKIT provides an efficient, easy to use, and readily scalable approach for the tagging of endogenous proteins to facilitate their study in intact biological systems.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion stated in the introduction.

claim: Homology Independent Target Integration (HITI) based KI strategies have been used to tag endogenous proteins in postmitotic cells such as neurons.
source: Homology Independent Target Integration (HITI) based KI strategies have been used to tag endogenous proteins in postmitotic cells such as neurons (Gao et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2016; Willems et al., 2020); however, these approaches are sensitive to INDEL mutations as the coding sequence is directly edited.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing HITI methods.

claim: HITI-based approaches are sensitive to INDEL mutations as the coding sequence is directly edited.
source: Homology Independent Target Integration (HITI) based KI strategies have been used to tag endogenous proteins in postmitotic cells such as neurons (Gao et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2016; Willems et al., 2020); however, these approaches are sensitive to INDEL mutations as the coding sequence is directly edited.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of HITI methods.

claim: INDEL mutations are particularly problematic when labeling the N-terminal region of proteins.
source: This is particularly problematic when labeling the N-terminal region of proteins, where the introduction of INDELs will be most damaging.
evidence: This is stated as a specific concern for N-terminal tagging.

claim: In the vast majority of cases, a Cas9 cutting site is not present at exactly the desired site of insertion.
source: Additionally, in the vast majority of cases, a Cas9 cutting site is not present at exactly the desired site of insertion.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: The choice of guides with high cutting efficiency and good off-target scores near the desired insertion site is often very limited.
source: Further, the choice of guides with high cutting efficiency and good off-target scores near the desired insertion site is often very limited.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: TKIT utilizes two guide RNAs that cut the genomic DNA flanking the coding region of interest.
source: Our approach utilizes two guide RNAs that cut the genomic DNA flanking the coding region of interest and includes a replacement donor DNA fragment encoding the excised coding sequence with the addition of a fluorescent or small (i.e., Myc) protein tag.
evidence: This is the core design of TKIT described in the Results section.

claim: The TKIT donor DNA fragment encodes the excised coding sequence with the addition of a fluorescent or small protein tag.
source: Our approach utilizes two guide RNAs that cut the genomic DNA flanking the coding region of interest and includes a replacement donor DNA fragment encoding the excised coding sequence with the addition of a fluorescent or small (i.e., Myc) protein tag.
evidence: This is part of the TKIT design described in the Results section.

claim: Guides for TKIT were designed to cut within the 5'-UTR and intron 1–2 of Gria2, located ~100 bp away from splice junctions.
source: We designed guides to cut within the 5'-UTR (untranslated region) and intron 1–2 of Gria2, choosing guides located ~100 bp away from splice junctions so as not to affect mRNA processing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is described in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Guides were located ~100 bp away from splice junctions so as not to affect mRNA processing.
source: We designed guides to cut within the 5'-UTR (untranslated region) and intron 1–2 of Gria2, choosing guides located ~100 bp away from splice junctions so as not to affect mRNA processing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a design consideration stated in the Results section.

claim: The TKIT donor DNA fragment contains the endogenous Gria2 sequence with the addition of a SEP-tag behind the signal peptide.
source: We constructed a donor DNA fragment containing the endogenous Gria2 sequence, with the addition of a SEP-tag behind the signal peptide, and the same two guides and PAM sequences at the ends.
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: The two guides within the TKIT donor have opposite locations and flipped sequences compared to the genomic DNA.
source: The two guides within the donor have opposite locations and flipped sequences compared to the genomic DNA (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is described in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The switch-and-flip design promotes forward insertion of the donor DNA.
source: We added this switch-and-flip design to promote forward insertion of the donor DNA, which occurs randomly through the process of NHEJ.
evidence: This is stated as the purpose of the switch-and-flip design.

claim: If the donor inserts in the reverse orientation without INDELs, the guides and PAMs remain intact so they will be cut again by Cas9.
source: If the donor inserts into the genome in the reverse orientation (and without INDELs) the guides and PAMs remain intact so they will be cut again by Cas9, enabling another chance at insertion in the correct orientation.
evidence: This is the mechanism by which the switch-and-flip design works.

claim: The cycle of cutting and re-insertion continues until the donor is inserted in the correct orientation, or until INDELs destroy the guides and PAM sequence.
source: The cycle will continue until the donor is inserted in the correct orientation, or until INDELs destroy the guides and PAM sequence (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is the mechanism by which TKIT achieves correct orientation insertion.

claim: Primary mouse cortical cultures were transfected at DIV7-9 with TKIT plasmids and mCherry as a cell morphology marker.
source: To test TKIT we transfected primary mouse cortical cultures at DIV7-9 with plasmids containing: (1) both guide RNAs along with SpCas9, (2) SEP-GluA2 donor DNA fragment, and (3) mCherry as a cell morphology marker (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is the experimental procedure described in the Results section.

claim: At DIV14-16, transfected neurons showed punctate SEP signal concentrated in dendritic spines, consistent with the labeling of AMPARs.
source: At DIV14-16 we live-imaged transfected neurons and found neurons with punctate SEP signal concentrated in dendritic spines, consistent with the labeling of AMPARs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is the result of the TKIT experiment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Immunofluorescence with antibodies against GFP and the C-terminus of GluA2 showed that the GFP signal was co-localized with GluA2.
source: We used immunofluorescence with antibodies against GFP and the C-terminus of GluA2 to show that the GFP signal was co-localized with GluA2 (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F-G demonstrating co-localization.

claim: Sequencing results showed that the splice junctions between exon1 and exon2 were intact, indicating that SEP KI did not affect Gria2 mRNA splicing.
source: Sequencing results showed that the splice junctions between exon1 and exon2 were intact, indicating that SEP KI did not affect Gria2 mRNA splicing (Figure 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with sequencing data.

claim: The expression level of SEP-GluA2 is comparable with GluA2 in non-transfected surrounding neurons.
source: Immunostaining of GluA2 in primary cultured neurons with TKIT mediated SEP-GluA2 KI showed that the expression level of SEP-GluA2 is comparable with GluA2 in non-transfected surrounding neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B with quantification.

claim: KI was dependent on co-transfection of the TKIT donor and the Cas9 with two guides constructs.
source: KI was dependent on co-transfection of the TKIT donor and the Cas9 with two guides constructs, as transfection of the TKIT donor alone did not lead to any detectable KI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C demonstrating the requirement for both components.

claim: Transfection of the TKIT donor alone did not lead to any detectable KI.
source: KI was dependent on co-transfection of the TKIT donor and the Cas9 with two guides constructs, as transfection of the TKIT donor alone did not lead to any detectable KI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C as a control experiment.

claim: NMDA and AMPA receptors mediate the majority of excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian CNS.
source: NMDA and AMPA receptors mediate the majority of excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian CNS and are critical for the tuning of synaptic strength.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: NMDA and AMPA receptors are critical for the tuning of synaptic strength.
source: NMDA and AMPA receptors mediate the majority of excitatory synaptic transmission in the mammalian CNS and are critical for the tuning of synaptic strength.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The trafficking of AMPA receptors is known to underlie synaptic plasticity, supporting learning, and memory.
source: In particular, the trafficking of AMPA receptors is known to underlie synaptic plasticity, supporting learning, and memory (Diering and Huganir, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diering and Huganir, 2018.

claim: The vast majority of AMPA receptor imaging studies have relied on the overexpression of tagged receptors.
source: To date, the vast majority of AMPA receptor imaging studies have relied on the overexpression of (often SEP) tagged receptors (Ashby et al., 2006; Kopec et al., 2006; Lin and Huganir, 2007; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers using overexpression approaches.

claim: There is concern that overexpression could result in aberrant and non-physiological receptor regulation.
source: While these studies have helped us learn about the regulation of AMPA receptors in vitro, and more recently, in vivo (Roth et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2015), there is always the concern that overexpression could result in aberrant and non-physiological receptor regulation.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of overexpression approaches.

claim: Tools to tag endogenous AMPARs will be highly useful.
source: Therefore, tools to tag endogenous AMPARs will be highly useful.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for developing TKIT.

claim: TKIT constructs were designed for SEP KI to the N-terminus of AMPAR subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3.
source: We designed TKIT constructs for SEP KI to the N-terminus of AMPAR subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3, as well as the most abundant NMDAR subunits (NR1, NR2A, and NR2B) and the beta2 subunit of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor.
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: TKIT constructs were designed for SEP KI to the N-terminus of NMDAR subunits NR1, NR2A, and NR2B.
source: We designed TKIT constructs for SEP KI to the N-terminus of AMPAR subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3, as well as the most abundant NMDAR subunits (NR1, NR2A, and NR2B) and the beta2 subunit of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor.
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: TKIT constructs were designed for SEP KI to the beta2 subunit of the GABA receptor.
source: We designed TKIT constructs for SEP KI to the N-terminus of AMPAR subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3, as well as the most abundant NMDAR subunits (NR1, NR2A, and NR2B) and the beta2 subunit of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor.
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: Gephyrin was targeted for GFP KI as a candidate cytosolic protein.
source: In addition, we wanted to demonstrate that TKIT also works for cytosolic proteins. To do this we targeted gephyrin, a postsynaptic scaffold protein that is localized to inhibitory synapses, as a candidate for GFP KI.
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: Gephyrin is a postsynaptic scaffold protein that is localized to inhibitory synapses.
source: In addition, we wanted to demonstrate that TKIT also works for cytosolic proteins. To do this we targeted gephyrin, a postsynaptic scaffold protein that is localized to inhibitory synapses, as a candidate for GFP KI.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gephyrin.

claim: Previous reports tagged the N-terminus of gephyrin.
source: Since previous reports tagged the N-terminus of gephyrin (Lardi-Studler et al., 2007; Tyagarajan et al., 2011), we also targeted GFP KI to the N-terminus of gephyrin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lardi-Studler et al., 2007 and Tyagarajan et al., 2011.

claim: Guide cutting sites for TKIT were located either in introns flanking the target exon, or in the 5'UTR of the targeted exon and the downstream intron.
source: To target this set of synaptic proteins, guide cutting sites were located either in introns flanking the target exon, or in the 5'UTR of the targeted exon and the downstream intron (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SEP-GluA1-3 signal in neurons showed clear puncta at dendritic spines.
source: The SEP-GluA1-3 signal in neurons, visualized with GFP immunostaining, showed clear puncta at dendritic spines (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: GFP-gephyrin and SEP-Beta2 showed punctate signals along dendrites.
source: As expected, GFP-gephyrin (Figure 2D) and SEP-Beta2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) showed punctate signals along dendrites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The efficiency for SEP KI to GluA1 was 21.9%.
source: The efficiency for SEP KI to AMPA receptor subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3 was 21.9%, 38.9%, and 20.5%, respectively (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with quantification.

claim: The efficiency for SEP KI to GluA2 was 38.9%.
source: The efficiency for SEP KI to AMPA receptor subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3 was 21.9%, 38.9%, and 20.5%, respectively (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F with quantification.

claim: The efficiency for SEP KI to GluA3 was 20.5%.
source: The efficiency for SEP KI to AMPA receptor subunits GluA1, GluA2, and GluA3 was 21.9%, 38.9%, and 20.5%, respectively (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G with quantification.

claim: The efficiency for Beta2 KI was 27.2%.
source: The efficiency for Beta2 KI was 27.2% (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and 41.7% for GFP-gephyrin KI (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B with quantification.

claim: The efficiency for GFP-gephyrin KI was 41.7%.
source: The efficiency for Beta2 KI was 27.2% (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and 41.7% for GFP-gephyrin KI (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2H with quantification.

claim: SEP-NR1, SEP-NR2A, and SEP-NR2B showed spine enrichment.
source: Targeting NMDA receptors resulted in similar spine enrichment for SEP-NR1, SEP-NR2A, and SEP-NR2B (Figure 3A–C) with efficiencies of 15.2%, 16.7%, and 27.5%, respectively (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The efficiency for SEP-NR1 KI was 15.2%.
source: Targeting NMDA receptors resulted in similar spine enrichment for SEP-NR1, SEP-NR2A, and SEP-NR2B (Figure 3A–C) with efficiencies of 15.2%, 16.7%, and 27.5%, respectively (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with quantification.

claim: The efficiency for SEP-NR2A KI was 16.7%.
source: Targeting NMDA receptors resulted in similar spine enrichment for SEP-NR1, SEP-NR2A, and SEP-NR2B (Figure 3A–C) with efficiencies of 15.2%, 16.7%, and 27.5%, respectively (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E with quantification.

claim: The efficiency for SEP-NR2B KI was 27.5%.
source: Targeting NMDA receptors resulted in similar spine enrichment for SEP-NR1, SEP-NR2A, and SEP-NR2B (Figure 3A–C) with efficiencies of 15.2%, 16.7%, and 27.5%, respectively (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with quantification.

claim: TKIT was used to KI tdTomato to Gephyrin and GluA2.
source: In addition to SEP, we used TKIT to KI the larger fluorescent protein tdTomato to Gephyrin (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and GluA2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) as well as the smaller tag Myc to GluA1 and GluA2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: TKIT was used to KI Myc tag to GluA1 and GluA2.
source: In addition to SEP, we used TKIT to KI the larger fluorescent protein tdTomato to Gephyrin (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and GluA2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) as well as the smaller tag Myc to GluA1 and GluA2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Correlation analysis showed strong correlation between the intensities of anti-GFP signal and anti-GluA1-3 signal in TKIT-mediated SEP KI neurons.
source: Correlation analysis showed strong correlation between the intensities of anti-GFP signal and anti-GluA1-3 signal in TKIT-mediated SEP KI neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6D-F with correlation plots.

claim: SEP-GluA1-3 showed synaptic localization verified by colocalization with PSD95.
source: We further validated the correct subcellular localization of proteins tagged with TKIT. We verified the synaptic localization of SEP-GluA1-3 with immunofluorescence using antibodies against GFP and PSD95 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: There was a strong correlation between the anti-GFP signal and anti-PSD95 signal in SEP KI neurons.
source: We observed a strong correlation between the anti-GFP signal and anti-PSD95 signal in SEP KI neurons (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D-F with correlation plots.

claim: GFP- or tdTomato-gephyrin signal colocalized with gephyrin and the GABA receptor Beta2 subunit.
source: We found that GFP- or tdTomato-gephyrin signal colocalized with gephyrin and the GABA receptor Beta2 subunit, used as a marker for inhibitory synapses (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Sequence analysis of reverse-transcribed cDNA showed intact splicing of all tagged proteins in this study.
source: Sequence analysis of reverse-transcribed cDNA from mRNA extracted from neuronal cultures electroporated with each TKIT construct showed intact splicing of all tagged proteins in this study (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with sequencing data.

claim: It is possible that a portion of exon 1 is excised and repaired without the addition of the donor DNA fragment, leading to the generation of a knock-out (KO) allele.
source: Because guides flank a critical portion of the gene being edited, it is possible that a portion of exon 1 is excised and repaired without the addition of the donor DNA fragment. This would lead to the generation of a knock-out (KO) allele for the target gene.
evidence: This is stated as a potential concern with TKIT.

claim: Genomic PCR showed clear KI and WT bands, but no detectable KO band.
source: DNA electrophoresis of the PCR products showed clear KI and WT bands, but no detectable KO band (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: GluA2 was not detectable in 12.4% of the mCherry-positive cells, indicating knock-out of GluA2 in a small subset of cells that failed to knock-in the donor DNA.
source: GluA2 was not detectable in 12.4% of the mCherry-positive cells, indicating knock-out of GluA2 in a small subset of cells that failed to knock-in the donor DNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D with quantification.

claim: 1.2% of cells had undetectable GluA2 in control experiments without TKIT manipulation.
source: To test the possibility that a subset of neurons naturally lacked GluA2 expression, independent of manipulation, we assessed the levels of GluA2 in mouse cortical neurons. We found that 1.2% of cells had undetectable GluA2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C with quantification.

claim: Plasmids containing SEP-GluA2 donor DNA and complementary two guides with spCas9 were transfected into layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of somatosensory cortex using in utero electroporation at E15.
source: Plasmids containing SEP-GluA2 donor DNA and complementary two guides with spCas9 were transfected into layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of somatosensory cortex using in utero electroporation of mouse embryos at embryonic day 15 (E15; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is the experimental procedure described in the Results section.

claim: Punctate SEP-GluA2 could be clearly observed along the dendrites of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in vivo.
source: Punctate SEP-GluA2 could be clearly observed along the dendrites of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—video 1), similar to previously studies showing the over-expressed SEP-GluA1 and SEP-GluA2 (Suresh and Dunaevsky, 2017; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: SEP signal was observed in mice that were more than 1-year old, indicating the long-term stability of the knock-in tag.
source: We were even able to observe SEP signal in mice that were more than 1-year old, indicating the long-term stability of the knock-in tag.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the in vivo experiments.

claim: A two-virus system was developed to enable genomic editing of wild-type mice.
source: We developed a two-virus system to enable genomic editing of wild-type mice.
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: HA-spCas9 was packaged into AAV.
source: We packaged HA-spCas9 into AAV and designed and produced AAVs to deliver two guides and donor DNA fragments within the same construct for SEP KI of GluA1 or GluA2 (TKIT-SEP-GluA1, TKIT-SEP-GluA2) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: AAVs were designed to deliver two guides and donor DNA fragments within the same construct for SEP KI of GluA1 or GluA2.
source: We packaged HA-spCas9 into AAV and designed and produced AAVs to deliver two guides and donor DNA fragments within the same construct for SEP KI of GluA1 or GluA2 (TKIT-SEP-GluA1, TKIT-SEP-GluA2) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: Native SEP fluorescence signal could be clearly detected in the injected hemisphere of the hippocampus.
source: We injected a mix of high titer AAV-spCas9 and AAV-TKIT-SEP-GluA2 into the dorsal hippocampus of adult C57BL/6 mice and allowed 3 weeks for AAV transduction, guide expression, genome editing/KI, and turnover/replacement of endogenous protein. Native SEP fluorescence signal could be clearly detected in the injected hemisphere of the hippocampus (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Of the HA-positive cells, 16.1% were also KI positive.
source: To calculate the efficiency of KI we used immunohistochemistry against HA to detect Cas9, and GFP to detect KI cells (Figure 5G). Of the HA-positive cells we found that 16.1% were also KI positive (Figure 5H), indicating high efficiency of genome editing in vivo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H with quantification.

claim: Camk2aCre or PvalbCre mice were bred with conditional Cas9 animals to generate offspring with Cas9 expression in forebrain CamK2a positive neurons or Pvalb positive interneurons.
source: To gain cell-type specificity of TKIT KI we bred heterozygous Camk2aCre or homozygous PvalbCre mice with homozygous lox-stop-lox conditional Cas9 animals to generate offspring with Cas9 expression in forebrain CamK2a positive neurons or Pvalb (PV) positive interneurons (Camk2aCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt or PvalbCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt).
evidence: This is the experimental procedure described in the Results section.

claim: Robust KI of SEP-GluA1 was observed in the dorsal hippocampus of the injected hemisphere after 2–3 weeks.
source: We injected high titer AAV-TKIT-SEP-GluA1 into the dorsal hippocampus of adult Camk2aCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt and PvalbCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt animals (Figure 6A,C). After 2–3 weeks we observed robust KI of SEP-GluA1 in the dorsal hippocampus of the injected hemisphere.
evidence: This is described in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Endogenous SEP signal could be seen concentrated in putative dendritic spines of excitatory neurons in Camk2aCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt animals.
source: Here, endogenous SEP signal could be seen concentrated in putative dendritic spines of excitatory neurons (Camk2aCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt animals) and along the smooth dendrites of PV neurons (PvalbCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt animals).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Endogenous SEP signal could be seen along the smooth dendrites of PV neurons in PvalbCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt animals.
source: Here, endogenous SEP signal could be seen concentrated in putative dendritic spines of excitatory neurons (Camk2aCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt animals) and along the smooth dendrites of PV neurons (PvalbCre/wt:Cas9fl/wt animals).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cells with SEP-GluA2 KI could be clearly observed in vivo with two-photon microscopy after AAV injection.
source: After 2 weeks, animals were imaged with two-photon microscopy. As with in utero electroporation, we could clearly observe cells with SEP-GluA2 KI in vivo (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Recent reports show that fragments of AAVs can integrate into double stranded DNA breaks induced by CRISPR/Cas9.
source: Recent reports show that fragments of AAVs can integrate into double stranded DNA breaks induced by CRISPR/Cas9 (Hanlon et al., 2019; Wolter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanlon et al., 2019 and Wolter et al., 2020.

claim: Integration of AAV fragments into the 5'UTR of GluA1 or GluA2 could disrupt function, potentially contributing to the decreased efficiency observed in vivo compared to in vitro.
source: Integration of AAV fragments into the 5'UTR of GluA1 or GluA2 could disrupt function, potentially contributing to the decreased efficiency observed in vivo (Figure 5H) compared to in vitro (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated as a potential explanation for the difference in efficiency.

claim: TKIT guides and donors were re-designed to be complementary to the rat genome to enable tagging of rat GluA1 and GluA2 with SEP.
source: We re-designed TKIT guides and donors to be complementary to the rat genome, to enable tagging of rat GluA1 and GluA2 with SEP.
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: Green puncta were observed at dendritic spines in rat neurons, which co-localized with the synaptic marker PSD95.
source: As expected, we observed green puncta at dendritic spines, which co-localized with the synaptic marker PSD95 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TKIT can mediate editing of the rat genome with efficiencies roughly equivalent to those observed in mouse neurons.
source: This demonstrates that TKIT can also mediate editing of the rat genome, with efficiencies roughly equivalent to those observed in mouse neurons (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and D with quantification.

claim: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) is a frequently used technique to assess the trafficking and mobility of proteins.
source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) is a frequently used technique to assess the trafficking and mobility of proteins (Ashby et al., 2006; Roth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers using FRAP.

claim: A recovery of the SEP-GluA1 signal was observed over time after photobleaching.
source: As expected for receptors that are constantly undergoing recycling to and from the synapse (Arendt et al., 2010; Frischknecht et al., 2009; Heine et al., 2008; Kerr and Blanpied, 2012; Makino and Malinow, 2009), we observed a recovery of the SEP-GluA1 signal over time (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The time constant for fluorescence recovery was estimated to be τ = 3.057 min.
source: Pooling the FRAP data from many spines (46 spines from three cells and three coverslips) enabled us to estimate the time constant for fluorescence recovery to be τ = 3.057 min, and the immobile fraction of receptors to be 52.44% under baseline conditions (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F with quantification.

claim: The immobile fraction of receptors was estimated to be 52.44% under baseline conditions.
source: Pooling the FRAP data from many spines (46 spines from three cells and three coverslips) enabled us to estimate the time constant for fluorescence recovery to be τ = 3.057 min, and the immobile fraction of receptors to be 52.44% under baseline conditions (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F with quantification.

claim: These findings are comparable to some, but not all, previous reports utilizing overexpression of SEP-GluA1.
source: These findings are comparable to some (Heine et al., 2008; Kerr and Blanpied, 2012), but not all (Makino and Malinow, 2009), previous reports utilizing overexpression of SEP-GluA1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers with similar and different findings.

claim: Very high levels of overexpression may increase the mobile pool of AMPARs beyond what is observed under more physiological conditions.
source: We speculate that this is critically dependent on the degree of overexpression, with very high levels of overexpression increasing the mobile pool of AMPARs beyond what is observed under more physiological conditions.
evidence: This is stated as speculation to explain differences with previous studies.

claim: Strategies to efficiently and reliably edit genomic DNA in post mitotic cells are lacking behind methods based on HDR that are routinely applied to dividing cells.
source: Strategies to efficiently, and reliably, edit genomic DNA in post mitotic cells, such as neurons, are lacking behind methods based on HDR that are routinely applied to dividing cells (Wang et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing HDR methods in dividing cells.

claim: Existing NHEJ-based methods have shown promise for enabling KI of tags to endogenous proteins in neurons.
source: Existing methods, based on NHEJ, have shown promise for enabling KI of tags (fluorescent proteins/small epitopes) to endogenous proteins in neurons (Gao et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2016); however, such methods are sensitive to INDEL mutations during the KI process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing NHEJ-based methods.

claim: Existing NHEJ-based methods are sensitive to INDEL mutations during the KI process.
source: Existing methods, based on NHEJ, have shown promise for enabling KI of tags (fluorescent proteins/small epitopes) to endogenous proteins in neurons (Gao et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2016); however, such methods are sensitive to INDEL mutations during the KI process.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing NHEJ-based methods.

claim: INDEL sensitivity culminates in reduced KI efficiency and generally restricts the locations where tags can be inserted within the target protein, typically limited to the C-terminal region.
source: This culminates in reduced KI efficiency and generally restricts the locations where tags can be inserted within the target protein, typically limited to the C-terminal region.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of INDEL sensitivity in existing methods.

claim: Recent studies have shown that residual HDR activity or introducing exogenous recombinase in neurons is capable of inducing KI.
source: Although recent studies have shown that residual HDR activity or introducing exogenous recombinase in neurons is capable of inducing KI (Cai et al., 2019; Nishiyama et al., 2017), the efficiency of such methods remains reasonably low, prompting us to develop alternative strategies for KI to neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2019 and Nishiyama et al., 2017.

claim: The efficiency of HDR or recombinase-based methods in neurons remains reasonably low.
source: Although recent studies have shown that residual HDR activity or introducing exogenous recombinase in neurons is capable of inducing KI (Cai et al., 2019; Nishiyama et al., 2017), the efficiency of such methods remains reasonably low, prompting us to develop alternative strategies for KI to neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of HDR/recombinase methods.

claim: Using TKIT, a tag can be inserted into any user-defined location without undesired amino acid loss or addition.
source: Using TKIT, a tag can be inserted into any user-defined location without undesired amino acid loss or addition.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: By using a pair of guide RNAs instead of a single guide RNA, TKIT utilizes Cas9 cutting sites that lie in non-coding regions of the gene of interest.
source: By using a pair of guide RNAs instead of a single guide RNA, TKIT utilizes the use of Cas9 cutting sites that lie in non-coding regions of the gene of interest (such as 5'-UTR and introns).
evidence: This is the core design principle of TKIT described in the Discussion.

claim: TKIT is significantly less sensitive to INDEL mutations since no coding regions of the gene are cut.
source: This approach is significantly less sensitive to INDEL mutations since no coding regions of the gene are cut.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: Even if INDELs are introduced around the cut sites with TKIT, it is highly likely that the mRNA and subsequent protein are left intact.
source: Even if INDELs are introduced around the cut sites, it is highly likely that the mRNA and subsequent protein are left intact.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: The switch-and-flip design built into the donor DNA sequence helps to bias the insertion of donor DNA into the correct orientation, further increasing KI efficiency.
source: Finally, the switch-and-flip design built into the donor DNA sequence helps to bias the insertion of donor DNA into the correct orientation, further increasing KI efficiency.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: The KI efficiency of SEP-GluA2 reached 16.1% in vivo with a two-virus system.
source: The KI efficiency of SEP-GluA2 reached 16.1% in vivo with a two-virus system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The in vivo KI efficiency with TKIT is greater than the efficiency achieved with the original demonstration of HITI.
source: This is greater than the efficiency achieved with the original demonstration of HITI (Suzuki et al., 2016; Nishiyama et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous methods, supported by citations.

claim: TKIT is particularly useful for tagging proteins at the N-terminus because of the increased protection from INDEL mutations.
source: Furthermore, because of the increased protection from INDEL mutations TKIT is particularly useful for tagging proteins at the N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: The pH sensitivity of SEP can be utilized to visualize the surface pool of receptors when the SEP-tag is positioned on the extracellular portion of the receptor.
source: Exploiting this, we were able to successfully KI SEP to the N-terminus of AMPA and NMDA receptor subunits, positioning the SEP-tag on the extracellular portion of the receptor so the pH sensitivity of SEP (Miesenböck et al., 1998) can be utilized to visualize the surface pool of receptors.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of N-terminal tagging with SEP, supported by citation.

claim: While TKIT is resistant to INDELs in the coding region of the gene being edited, the method is not immune to other caveats.
source: While TKIT is resistant to INDELs in the coding region of the gene being edited, the method is not immune to other caveats.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: If the donor DNA is not present to replace the excised genomic DNA then a KO allele could be generated.
source: For example, if the donor DNA (with the tag/label) is not present to replace the excised genomic DNA then a KO allele could be generated.
evidence: This is stated as a potential caveat of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: For GluA2 tagging with SEP, KO of GluA2 was observed in 12.4% of transfected cells.
source: For GluA2 tagging with SEP we observed KO of GluA2 in 12.4% of transfected cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: It will be important to consider that KI neurons are likely surrounded by a small fraction of neurons that are heterozygous or homozygous KO's for the gene of interest.
source: Therefore, it will be important to consider that KI neurons are likely surrounded by a small fraction of neurons that are heterozygous or homozygous KO's for the gene of interest.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration when using TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: TKIT KI of SEP to GluA2 is compatible with two-photon imaging in vivo.
source: In proof of principle experiments, we showed that TKIT KI of SEP to GluA2 is compatible with two-photon imaging in vivo, enabling us to visualize the surface expression of endogenous GluA2-containing AMPARs in live animals for the first time.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: TKIT enables visualization of the surface expression of endogenous GluA2-containing AMPARs in live animals for the first time.
source: In proof of principle experiments, we showed that TKIT KI of SEP to GluA2 is compatible with two-photon imaging in vivo, enabling us to visualize the surface expression of endogenous GluA2-containing AMPARs in live animals for the first time.
evidence: This is stated as a novel achievement in the Discussion.

claim: A lower efficiency of KI was observed in vivo (16.1%) compared to in vitro (38.9%) with SEP-GluA2.
source: While we observed a lower efficiency of KI in vivo (16.1%) compared to in vitro (38.9%) with SEP-GluA2, it is likely that we are under-representing the in vivo efficiency, as a proportion of the cells that were transduced with SpCas9 might have failed to receive the TKIT donor DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to data in Figures 5H and 2F.

claim: The in vivo efficiency may be under-represented because a proportion of cells transduced with SpCas9 might have failed to receive the TKIT donor DNA.
source: While we observed a lower efficiency of KI in vivo (16.1%) compared to in vitro (38.9%) with SEP-GluA2, it is likely that we are under-representing the in vivo efficiency, as a proportion of the cells that were transduced with SpCas9 might have failed to receive the TKIT donor DNA.
evidence: This is stated as a potential explanation for the lower in vivo efficiency.

claim: Tagging endogenous proteins to study their function and subcellular localization is preferential to exogenous protein overexpression.
source: Tagging endogenous proteins to study their function and subcellular localization is preferential to exogenous protein overexpression.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the Discussion.

claim: The adoption of endogenous KI strategies such as TKIT will dramatically aid the study of proteins expressed at physiological levels.
source: Therefore, the adoption of endogenous KI strategies such as TKIT will dramatically aid the study of proteins expressed at physiological levels.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: A potential application of TKIT is its combination with modern proximity labeling techniques such as APEX, BioID, and TurboID.
source: A potential application of TKIT is its combination with modern proximity labeling techniques such as APEX, BioID, and TurboID (Branon et al., 2018; Rhee et al., 2013; Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a potential application in the Discussion, supported by citations.

claim: Proximity labeling techniques crucially rely on proper subcellular targeting of fusion proteins.
source: Those techniques crucially rely on proper subcellular targeting of fusion proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for proximity labeling techniques.

claim: Tagging endogenous proteins with proximity labeling enzymes will reduce the confound of nonspecific subcellular protein localization associated with protein overexpression.
source: Tagging endogenous proteins with proximity labeling enzymes will reduce the confound of nonspecific subcellular protein localization associated with protein overexpression and increase the signal to noise ratio of 'hits' as there will be lower background from mis-localized proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a potential advantage of combining TKIT with proximity labeling.

claim: The feasibility of coupling TKIT with proximity labeling remains to be tested.
source: However, the feasibility of coupling TKIT with proximity labeling remains to be tested and will likely depend upon the transfection or transduction efficiency, the KI efficiency for the target protein, as well as the absolute abundance of the target protein being tagged.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat for the proposed application.

claim: The flexibility with where tags can be introduced will allow known protein interaction motifs to be avoided when tagging target proteins.
source: In addition, the flexibility with where tags can be introduced will be of great value as it will allow known protein interaction motifs (i.e., C-terminal PDZ ligands) to be avoided when tagging target proteins, further preventing mis-localization of the protein being studied.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TKIT in the Discussion.

claim: Faithful mRNA splicing of GluA2 was detected following TKIT SEP KI.
source: While we detect faithful mRNA splicing of GluA2 following TKIT SEP KI, it remains a potential concern that targeting non-coding regions could have unforeseen effects on mRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to sequencing data.

claim: It remains a potential concern that targeting non-coding regions could have unforeseen effects on mRNA processing.
source: While we detect faithful mRNA splicing of GluA2 following TKIT SEP KI, it remains a potential concern that targeting non-coding regions could have unforeseen effects on mRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated as a potential concern in the Discussion.

claim: A greater understanding of the biology underlying mRNA processing will facilitate the design of guides to avoid effects on mRNA processing.
source: A greater understanding of the biology underlying mRNA processing will facilitate the design of guides to avoid such effects.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction in the Discussion.

claim: Given the high flexibility in guide RNA choice, concerns about mRNA processing will be easily overcome.
source: Given the high flexibility in guide RNA choice, this concern will be easily overcome, as long as genomic DNA cutting sites can be identified that leave mRNA processing unaffected.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: TKIT is an efficient, reliable, and easy to implement method for tagging endogenous proteins in vitro and in vivo.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that TKIT is an efficient, reliable, and easy to implement method for tagging endogenous proteins in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: TKIT can edit mouse and rat genomic DNA.
source: TKIT can edit mouse and rat genomic DNA, with promised utility in all model organisms.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the Results section with data from mouse and rat neurons.

claim: TKIT has promised utility in all model organisms.
source: TKIT can edit mouse and rat genomic DNA, with promised utility in all model organisms.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: To date, TKIT has only been used to KI tags to proteins.
source: Although, to date, we have only used TKIT to KI tags to proteins, a potential application to clinical therapy to correct causative mutations in genetic disorders could be possible.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current applications in the Discussion.

claim: A potential application of TKIT to clinical therapy to correct causative mutations in genetic disorders could be possible.
source: Although, to date, we have only used TKIT to KI tags to proteins, a potential application to clinical therapy to correct causative mutations in genetic disorders could be possible.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future application in the Discussion.
